answers.answer: Fastify is a low-overhead Node.js web-server framework with routes, validation/serialization, logging, hooks and plugins. Application authors import its factory, register handlers and call listen; HTTP clients then invoke those routes through the Node server. Public tests likewise construct servers and make requests. It is a library consumed by applications, not a standalone application whose business handlers are fixed here.

fastify.js assembles the public instance and plugin lifecycle (Avvio/encapsulation). lib/server.js creates HTTP/HTTPS/HTTP2 servers and manages listening. lib/route.js registers routes with find-my-way and creates request/reply contexts. lib/request.js and lib/reply.js expose request/response APIs; Reply handles sending and serialization. lib/handle-request.js runs the request lifecycle; lib/wrap-thenable.js handles returned promises. Hooks/content-type-parser provide lifecycle extension and body parsing. schema-controller/validation/schemas manage schema storage and validator/serializer compilers; defaults use the Fastify AJV and fast-json-stringify compiler packages. Logger-factory and error-handler support logging and failures.

The production library is JavaScript/CommonJS on Node.js, packaged as npm fastify with main fastify.js and types fastify.d.ts; types/ supplies TypeScript declarations, with TypeScript examples/type tests. npm scripts use Node for generated validation/error-serializer builds, borp for unit tests, c8 for coverage, ESLint for linting and tstyche for type tests. The map shows one principal root package and separate esbuild/webpack package manifests under test/bundler, which are test fixtures rather than separate production services. An integration shell script is also present.

Begin with require('fastify')(options), or import the default/named fastify factory and call it. package.json points to fastify.js; its fastify(serverOptions) factory starts at line 89, processes options, builds routing and creates the server. The factory is exported directly and through .fastify/.default. Applications then register routes and call listen.

X is lib/wrap-thenable.js, wrapThenable's fulfillment callback (14-53), which calls reply.send(payload). lib/handle-request.js invokes wrapThenable at line 206 after detecting a thenable returned by the configured handler. Hijacked replies are skipped; an undefined result is sent only when the reply/headers are unsent and the request/socket remains live.

Seven direct internal dependencies, all proven by outgoing require declarations: wrap-thenable (4), validation (5), hooks (6), errors (7-10), error-status (11), symbols (12-19), content-type (20). Direction is handle-request.js → required module, not the reverse. node:diagnostics_channel is an additional Node built-in, not an internal module.

With no prior error/sent reply: handleRequest → handler → optional preValidation hooks → preValidationCallback → validateSchema → validationCompleted → optional preHandler hooks → preHandlerCallback → preHandlerCallbackInner → context.handler → wrapThenable → fulfillment callback → reply.send(payload). Dynamic boundaries are configured hooks/validators, context.handler, promise scheduling, diagnostics runStores and receiver-dispatched reply.send. Validation/errors or an already-sent reply can stop progression; hijack or an undefined payload with a non-live/already-sent response suppresses automatic sending.

Two direct production consumers: lib/route.js requires the exported handleRequest function (line 5), using it from runPreParsing; lib/reply.js requires the Symbol.for('internals') export (line 36), using preHandlerCallback for not-found processing. Test consumers also exist but are outside the requested production set. This is the complete direct static-import set returned by the module's map incoming edges, not an assertion about arbitrary runtime require calls.

test/async-await.test.js, test('async await'), exercises X publicly. It requires '..', constructs Fastify(), registers GET '/' with async awaitMyFunc (49-52) that waits and returns {hello:'world'}, and also registers an immediately resolving async '/no-await'. It listens on port 0, fetches both routes, and checks HTTP 200, content-length and returned JSON. Thus it enters through the package factory, public route registration and actual HTTP requests, rather than directly invoking wrapThenable. I inspected this test; I did not execute it.

Public registration can start at fastify.query, which delegates a QUERY route to prepareRoute (204-206); QUERY belongs to the default bodywith set. A matched request runs routeHandler/onRequest → runPreParsing → handleRequest. There, missing Content-Type on QUERY sets kReplyIsError and sends status 400 with FST_ERR_ROUTE_MISSING_CONTENT_TYPE(method), returning before parsing, validation or the route handler—even if no body was supplied. This assumes earlier hooks have not already replied/failed.
